title: What I Learned from Reducing my Email Inbox from About a Million* Messages to Zero
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes how a school year of anxious, compulsive email checking left him with roughly 500 messages in each of his school and personal inboxes, and how he cleared both. For the school inbox he used a blunt reset: answer what truly needs an answer, then archive everything else, on the premise that most school email never serves students' long-term flourishing. For the personal inbox he followed a Merlin Mann style purge in six waves covering deletion, forwarding, two-minute replies, moving tasks to an index card, culling newsletters, and mopping up. The piece's sharper insight is that his inbox was doing two jobs at once, as a chemical fix and a to-do list, and that perfectionism about long replies had meant no replies at all. He closes by promising a follow-up on a sustainable email practice built on discipline and dignity.
points: Email is a satisficing zone for teachers: most messages do not need a reply, so archiving en masse costs little compared with the attention it frees.
Perfectionism about writing the 'right' long reply produced months of silence; a quick two-minute answer today beats a thorough one never.
An inbox with no defined purpose, used as both dopamine source and to-do list, generates anxiety; moving tasks to a real list separates the two.
The six-wave purge gives a practical order of attack: delete, forward, answer fast, list tasks, prune subscriptions, then handle the remainder.
quotes: For pretty much all of last school year, my inbox was a nightmare. Every time I’d open it, I’d get this messed up chemical cocktail released into my brain: one part excitement, one part anxiety. I became addicted to checking it on my phone, tapping the little mail app a dozen or more times per day, and I became really good at pushing down the gut-squirmy feelings that came when the little Red Numbers of Death floating over the email icon kept growing.

If there’s anything satisfice-worthy in a teacher’s daily life, it’s probably email. Email is crazy, and few of the emails we receive every day will actually help us get our kids closer to long-term flourishing.

In other words, yes, I probably missed a few emails that needed responses — but then again, if I still have my job and there aren’t any parents or students egging my house this summer (yet), did those emails really need responses?

Here was a classic case of self-sabotaging perfectionism: in waiting for the “right time” to sit down and write what I felt was the appropriately long response to a reader email, I had actually just not responded at all, and in some cases this not responding had been going on for months. Note to self: in the future, people would probably prefer a two-minute response today over a twenty-minute response never.

My inbox, like many inboxes in the world, was partially screwed up because of my lack of clarity around its purpose. I was using it as both a chemical fix (checking for new messages on my phone) as well as a to-do list (marking messages that I checked on my phone but needed to do something about as “Unread”). So I took out the to-do list-ish emails and put them on an actual to-do list index card.

Basically, I realized I was subscribed to more newsletters than I wanted to read. So anything that I didn’t genuinely want to read every day — I could figure out a strategy for reading things more consistently later — I unsubscribed from. Things that I did want to read, I went old school and printed them out.
